passage: Naveen, five, burst through the door of their farmhouse near Amritsar, cap askew. "Papa Suraj Papa I saw a tractor with a huge tyre and it was going in the mud and the driver waved and the dog barked and I waved back and—" Suraj knelt, laughing. "Easy, easy. Tell me every part, one at a time." Naveen took a breath. "There was a... big tractor." "Yes?" "With a huge tyre. The driver waved." Suraj listened to each part, nodding, until the whole story unfolded.

qa.q: What did Naveen see with a huge tyre?
qa.a: He saw a tractor with a huge tyre going in the mud.

qa.q: What was Naveen feeling as his words tumbled out?
qa.a: He was excited and eager to share, and his words came in a rush with parts skipped. He may also have been afraid that Suraj would stop listening before the end.

qa.q: What worked in the way Suraj responded?
qa.a: He asked Naveen to tell every part one at a time and listened to each part, so Naveen could organise the story.

qa.q: How might Suraj feel as Naveen's story rushes out?
qa.a: He seems amused and fond, since he laughs, kneels and asks to hear every part, one at a time.

grounding: A preschooler with big news speaks in a rush, and a patient adult helps him organise his story.

passage: Ingrid, five, ran to the door of their Bergen flat. "Mamma, Rafael, at school we did a volcano and the red stuff came out and the teacher went back and the boy cried and it was so BIG—" Her brother Rafael, at the table with homework, grinned. "Wait, Ingrid. Start again." She took a breath. "We made a volcano." "And?" "The red stuff came out, and it went everywhere." She talked more slowly, and Rafael put his pencil down and said, "That's really cool."

qa.q: What did Ingrid's class make at school?
qa.a: They made a volcano.

qa.q: What was Ingrid feeling as she rushed through her news?
qa.a: She was very excited about the volcano and wanted to tell everything at once, so the words tumbled out. Her loud "BIG" suggests how much it thrilled her.

qa.q: What could Rafael do to help Ingrid tell her story?
qa.a: He can keep asking her to start again and prompt with short questions like "And?", as he did.

qa.q: How might Rafael feel about Ingrid's volcano news?
qa.a: He seems interested, since he puts his pencil down and says, "That's really cool."

grounding: A preschooler speaks in a rushed tumble when excited, and patient prompting helps her organise her story.

passage: At the swimming club, Sahil ran up to Farhan Sir dripping wet. “SirSirIswamtheIwentallthewayandnofloatandthenIputmyfaceandIdidn'tstop!” Farhan Sir laughed and crouched. “Slow down. I want every bit of it. What happened first?” Sahil took a big breath. “First I took off the float.” “Then?” “Then I put my face in.” “Then?” “Then I swam all the way to the rope!” Sir held up his hand for a high five. “All the way! That's big news.”

qa.q: What did Sahil take off first?
qa.a: The float.

qa.q: What does Sahil's tumble of words suggest he was feeling?
qa.a: It suggests he was very excited and proud about swimming all the way, so the words came out faster than he could order them.

qa.q: How did Farhan Sir help Sahil tell his story?
qa.a: He told Sahil to slow down because he wanted every bit of it, and asked “What happened first?” and “Then?” to help Sahil put it in order.

qa.q: How might Farhan Sir feel hearing the whole story?
qa.a: He likely feels proud of Sahil and happy to share his excitement. 😊

grounding: A preschooler rushes his big news, and his coach patiently helps him organise the story.

passage: I'm Vinita, from the next house. This morning Swati came running to her father at the gate, words spilling out: “Papa-the-cat-the-box-there's-babies-three-no-four-and-one-is-black-and-the-cat-licked-them!” He knelt down. “Slow down, I'd love to hear every bit. Where's the box?” She pointed. “Under the stairs.” “How many babies?” She counted on her fingers slowly. “Four.” I don't know how long she'd been watching, but she was glowing. They tiptoed off together to look.

qa.q: Where was the box?
qa.a: Under the stairs.

qa.q: What might Swati have been feeling as the words spilled out?
qa.a: She was very excited about the kittens, which is why she rushed and mixed up the number. Vinita couldn't be sure how long she'd been watching.

qa.q: What helped Swati organise her news?
qa.a: Her father told her to slow down, said he'd love to hear every bit, and asked simple questions one at a time.

qa.q: How did Vinita see the moment?
qa.a: Vinita noticed how excited and glowing Swati was, and how patient her father was in helping her.

grounding: A neighbour observes a preschooler rushing her news about kittens and her father helping her slow down and tell it in order.

passage:
Monday: Ishita burst in from school talking so fast Francis caught only “sticker” and “teacher” and “Riya cried.” He said, “Okay, okay,” while cooking. Ishita stopped and walked away.
Wednesday: She rushed in again. Francis turned off the stove. “Slow down, tell me everything. What happened first?”
Friday: Ishita came in, took a breath herself, and said, “First, the teacher gave stickers. Then Riya didn't get one and cried. Then I gave her mine.” Francis hugged her. “That was kind.”

qa.q: What did Ishita do with her sticker on Friday's story?
qa.a: She gave it to Riya.

qa.q: What was Ishita feeling when she stopped and walked away on Monday?
qa.a: She probably felt ignored and disappointed that her father wasn't really listening to her big news.

qa.q: What did Francis change on Wednesday, and why did it help?
qa.a: He stopped cooking, told her to slow down and tell him everything, and asked what happened first, which helped her order the story.

qa.q: How might Riya have felt when Ishita gave her the sticker?
qa.a: Riya would likely have felt happy and comforted after crying.

grounding: Over a week, a father's patient invitation to slow down and tell everything helps a preschooler organise her excited stories.

passage:
Manoj was at the bus stop with Minakshi, and their bus was already turning the corner.

"Papa-Papa-at-school-there-was-a-snake-no-not-a-real-one-yes-a-real-one-in-a-box-and-the-man-and-it-went-like-this-and-Teacher-screamed-and-"

"Whoa." Manoj held her hand as they climbed on. "Slow down, beti. I want every single bit. Start from the beginning, once we sit."

They found a seat. Minakshi took a breath.

"A man came to school. He brought a snake in a box. A real one."

"And then?"

"Then he took it out, and Teacher screamed!"

qa.q: What did the man bring to school?
qa.a: A snake in a box.

qa.q: What was Minakshi feeling when her words came out in a rushed tumble?
qa.a: She was most likely bursting with excitement about the snake visit, so her story came out jumbled with parts skipped. She may also have felt hurried because the bus was coming.

qa.q: How did Manoj help Minakshi tell her story?
qa.a: He said he wanted every bit of the story, asked her to start from the beginning once they sat, and asked "And then?" to help her order it.

qa.q: What would change if Manoj had said, "Not now, the bus is here"?
qa.a: Minakshi might have felt her big news did not matter, and her excitement could have turned into disappointment.

grounding: It shows a preschooler rushing her big news in a tumble of words and a patient adult helping her tell it in order.
